target_customer: Donors of surplus medicine (long-term care pharmacies, nursing homes, manufacturers, pharmacies) and safety-net clinics that serve uninsured and underinsured patients; funded by philanthropy and donor-side partners
problem: Billions of dollars of unexpired, unopened medicine are destroyed each year while many Americans skip prescriptions because of cost.
business_model: Nonprofit platform matching donated surplus medicine to clinics, funded by grants, donations and consulting to governments, clinics and donor groups

founders.name: Kiah J. Williams
founders.background_notes: Stanford GSB case says she started SIRUM as a Stanford undergraduate with Adam Kircher and George Wang.

founders.name: Adam Kircher
founders.background_notes: Named a co-founder on the YC page and in the Stanford GSB case.

founders.name: George Wang
founders.background_notes: Named a co-founder on the YC page and in the Stanford GSB case.

technical_complexity.rationale: A web matching and inventory platform between donors and clinics; the hard parts were compliance with state Good Samaritan and donation laws and pharmacy workflows, not software.

defensibility.rationale: Legal expertise across states, patented technology claim on its site and integrations with long-term care pharmacy workflows made replication slower than software alone.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent was found copying or buying it; it remains an independent nonprofit.

market_need_then: A 2014-era source reports state Good Samaritan style donation laws in 42 to 44 states and SIRUM had redistributed about 1 million pills worth about $3 million wholesale to serve about 20,000 patients by mid-2014; its site cites up to $11B of medicine wasted yearly and 50 million Americans skipping prescriptions for cost.

branding.name_origin: Acronym for Supporting Initiatives to Redistribute Unused Medicine, per Wikipedia and GuideStar search results (pages not opened).

identity.voice_and_tone: Mission driven; co-founder pitched it as a match.com for unused medicine

branding.brand_signature: The match.com for unused medicine line
branding.community_and_virality: Press features from Smithsonian magazine, Becker's Hospital Review and Fierce Healthcare per search results; no merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Trade and national press coverage and partnerships with large long-term care pharmacies show recognition in its niche, though the acronym has no meaning to outsiders.

outcome_analysis: SIRUM grew from a Stanford student project into what it calls the largest US redistributor of surplus medicine, with networks across five states and medicine donation embedded in the workflow of 7 of the top 10 long-term care pharmacy companies by March 2023 according to a DRK Foundation update. It relied on philanthropy rather than venture rounds, and a Stanford case says it had funding secured through 2025.
notes: Nonprofit, so venture style rounds do not apply. No verified grant amounts found. CB Insights lists about $490K across six rounds with a $0.28M grant in Nov 2020, Employbl lists a $120K YC seed, and InfluenceWatch reports revenue of about $33.8M in 2022 (likely includes in-kind donated medicine); all unverified and conflicting, so none recorded. Echoing Green and Philanthropic Ventures Foundation are named as grantors without amounts. Competitors empty because only unnamed traditional redistribution programs were referenced; a BounceWatch list was unreliable. Founding year 2009 comes from a search snippet, not opened.
